displayQuote: Religion is the opium of the people

meta.title: Who really said "Religion is the opium of the people"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Karl Marx, in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, Paris, February 1844. But he wrote ‘people’, not ‘masses’, and it’s two sentences fused.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Religion is the opium of the people'?
meta.ogDescription: Marx really wrote it — page 72 of a Paris journal, February 1844. The German says ‘Opium des Volks’: opium of the people, not opiate of the masses.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political theorist & revolutionary socialist
answer.sourceLine: Marx wrote it in the introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right, printed in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (Paris, February 1844). Page 72 of that first printing reads “Sie ist das Opium des Volks” — rendered “It is the opium of the people” in H. J. Stenning’s 1926 English translation ↗, so the famous one-liner is a faithful compression of Marx’s own words rather than a sentence he set down whole.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right — Introduction
Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, Paris: Bureau der Jahrbücher, February 1844, pp. 71–85 (the quote falls on p. 72)
H. J. Stenning, in Selected Essays (New York: International Publishers, 1926), p. 12

source.excerpt: Religious misery is in one mouth the expression of real misery, and in another is a protestation against real misery. Religion is the moan of the oppressed creature, the sentiment of a heartless world, as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions. It is the opium of the people.
trail: December 1843 – January 1844, Paris. Marx drafts an introduction to a critique of Hegel he will never finish. The Marxists Internet Archive dates the writing to those two months ↗.

February 1844. The introduction runs from page 71 of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher — the journal’s only issue, a double number ↗. The scan of page 72 carries the sentence: ‘Sie ist das Opium des Volks’ ↗.
1909. Lenin makes the line doctrine, writing that ‘this dictum by Marx is the corner-stone of the whole Marxist outlook on religion’ ↗.
1926, New York. The earliest English version we could verify against a scan appears in Selected Essays, translated by H. J. Stenning for International Publishers ↗.
source.cutTag: Stenning trans., Selected Essays (1926), p. 12 — from Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, Paris, 1844, p. 72
source.excerptNote: That is H. J. Stenning’s 1926 English, the earliest rendering we could check against a scan. Marx’s German on page 72 of the 1844 printing reads “Sie ist das Opium des Volks.” Later translators reached for warmer words — the widely reproduced modern version has “the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world” — but every version ends the same way, and in none of them is “Religion is the opium of the people” a single sentence Marx wrote.

sourceLink.text: Stenning’s 1926 translation, page 12, scan-backed on Wikisource

source.rightsNote: Both layers are clear. Marx’s German original was published in Paris in 1844 and has long been in the public domain. The English shown here is H. J. Stenning’s translation, first published in New York by International Publishers in 1926 — before 1931, so it is public domain in the United States too. Note that the more familiar modern English wording of this passage comes from a much later translation and is not public domain; that is why we quote the 1926 text.

author.name: Karl Marx
author.heading: Karl Marx
author.metaLine: 1818–1883 · German philosopher, political theorist & revolutionary socialist
author.bio: Karl Marx was a German philosopher, political theorist and revolutionary socialist who spent most of his adult life in exile — Paris, Brussels, and finally London, where he died in 1883. When this passage appeared he was in his Paris years, co-editing a short-lived radical journal with Arnold Ruge and working out the materialist account of history he would argue for the rest of his life. He is far better known for what came four years later, The Communist Manifesto, but the opium sentence is the one line of his that almost everybody can quote — usually slightly wrong.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Marx. Almost everything about how the sentence travels is a little wrong.

items.why: Marx’s German is Opium des Volks: opium, and Volk, the people. Wikipedia notes the line is often rendered ‘opiate of the masses’ ↗, and Phrase Finder lists ‘opiate of the masses’, ‘opium of the masses’ and ‘opium of the people’ as competing English versions, the last preferred by German scholars ↗. ‘Masses’ also imports a coolness towards ordinary people that Marx’s Volk does not carry.

items.who: One sentence that was really two
items.why: Marx never set down the string ‘Religion is the opium of the people.’ He wrote a sentence beginning ‘Religion is the moan of the oppressed creature…’ and then a short second one: ‘It is the opium of the people.’ Wikipedia describes the famous quotation as bits of two sentences run together ↗. The compression is fair to his meaning — but it is a compression.

items.who: Marx as the inventor of the metaphor
items.why: Wikipedia documents earlier uses ↗: Novalis wrote in 1798 that a certain sort of religion works like an opiate; Heinrich Heine in 1840 welcomed a religion that pours ‘spiritual opium’ into human suffering; and Bruno Bauer, a direct influence on this very essay, wrote of religion’s ‘opium-like’ effect. The same page records the Anglican canon Charles Kingsley reaching for the same image in 1847 — four years after Marx, not before him. Marx made it famous; he did not coin it.

Lenin did more than anyone to spread the line — in 1909 he wrote that ‘this dictum by Marx is the corner-stone of the whole Marxist outlook on religion’ ↗. His own blunter gloss now travels alongside it and is regularly mistaken for Marx’s: the sentence calling religion ‘a sort of spiritual booze’ is Lenin’s, from Novaya Zhizn in December 1905 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Marx did write it, and you can look at the page: page 72 of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, Paris, February 1844 — ‘Sie ist das Opium des Volks’ ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Read the sentences on either side and the metaphor changes shape. Marx calls religion the moan of the oppressed creature and, in the same breath, a protest against real misery — not a lie the powerful tell, but a sound the powerless make. The opium line is the last beat of that thought, and the paragraph immediately after recasts the abolition of religion as the demand for real happiness — calling on people to give up ‘a condition that requires illusions’.

It also helps to know what opium was in 1844: not only an intoxicant but the century’s workhorse medicine, the thing in the household cupboard for pain, fever and dysentery. Roland Boer argues the metaphor is widely misread for exactly this reason — that opium was then both valued and denounced, for its medicinal qualities and its addictive potential ↗. Read that way the sentence is a diagnosis rather than a sneer: real relief, and a reason not to look for a cure.
context.detailsSummary: How a line nobody read became the most quoted sentence Marx wrote
detailsBody: The journal was a flop. Only one issue of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher ever appeared, a double number ↗, and Wikipedia records a print run of just 1,000 copies and no popular effect during the 19th century ↗.

The phrase’s fame is therefore second-hand. Lenin made it the corner-stone of the Marxist position on religion ↗, and Wikipedia dates the phrase’s wider currency to the 1930s ↗ — by which time almost everyone meeting the sentence was meeting it without its paragraph.
context.pull: ‘Sie ist das Opium des Volks’ — six German words, and almost every English version of them is a paraphrase.

sourcesVerified.claim: Marx's introduction was written December 1843 – January 1844 and first published in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, 7 & 10 February 1844 in Paris; the text contains "It is the opium of the people."
The German original on page 72 of the 1844 first printing reads "...einer herzlosen Welt, wie sie der Geist geistloser Zustände ist. Sie ist das Opium des Volks."
The work page's bibliographic header gives: Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, pp. 71–85; publisher Bureau der Jahrbücher; Paris; 1844; edited by Arnold Ruge and Karl Marx; written 1843/44.

H. J. Stenning's English translation reads: "Religion is the moan of the oppressed creature, the sentiment of a heartless world, as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions. It is the opium of the people." — on the page footed as printed page 12.
The edition record for that scan gives: Selected Essays by Karl Marx, translator Henry James Stenning, publisher International Publishers, New York City, 1926 (OCLC 2829300, LCCN 26015348).

Wikiquote lists the passage ending "It is the opium of the people" in its sourced section under Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, and lists no opium entry under Disputed or Misattributed.

The line is often rendered "religion ... is the opiate of the masses"; the famous quotation is bits of two sentences run together; earlier users of the metaphor include Novalis (1798), Heinrich Heine (1840) and Bruno Bauer, while Charles Kingsley used it in 1847, "four years after Marx"; Lenin's Novaya Zhizn passage of 3 December 1905 calls religion "a sort of spiritual booze"; the journal had a print run of just 1,000 copies and no popular effect during the 19th century, the phrase becoming better known during the 1930s; Roland Boer argues the metaphor is misread because opium was then valued and denounced for its medicinal qualities and its addictive potential.
Lenin wrote: "Religion is the opium of the people—this dictum by Marx is the corner-stone of the whole Marxist outlook on religion."

The phrase "has been translated variously as 'religion is the opiate of the masses', 'religion is the opium of the masses' and, in a version which German scholars prefer 'religion is the opium of the people'", and is credited to Karl Marx.
The Deutsch–Französische Jahrbücher published only one issue, a double number, in February 1844, and Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right begins on page 71 of it.
Karl Marx was born 5 May 1818 in Trier and died 14 March 1883 in London; he is described as a German philosopher, social and political theorist, and revolutionary socialist.
